requested.title: Deployed site/demos image runs NODE_ENV=development, which degrades CSRF origin enforcement to warn-and-allow
Dev-mode deployment leaks stack traces and mounts three unauthenticated internal route families in production
Image enables an unauthenticated full V8 heap-dump endpoint that exposes MOCHI_KEY and all in-process secrets
Unauthenticated forced-GC endpoint enabled by MOCHI_MEMORY_PROBE allows cheap stop-the-world DoS
Production image resolves all dependencies without a lockfile, so builds are non-reproducible and unreviewed

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: Every link in the chain verifies. `.github/workflows/build.yml` sets `dockerfile: Dockerfile` for the `site` (L41-48) and `demos` (L53-59) legs and both are deployed to CapRover in the `deploy` job (L233-240). Dockerfile L79 is `ENTRYPOINT ["sh","-c","exec bun run dev:${WORKSPACE}"]`; root `dev:site`/`dev:demos` delegate to each workspace's `dev` script, and both `packages/site/package.json:14` and `packages/demos/package.json:11` are `NODE_ENV=development bun src/index.ts`. `utils/env.ts:12-17` makes `SEEDED_IS_DEV` true; `Mochi.ts:479` resolves `development` from it (site passes no `development`; demos passes `process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development'`, same result). `requestSetup.ts:62-64` sets `csrf: true` for `page` and `api` and L119-120 forwards `cfg.development` into `csrfCheck`, which lands at `csrf.ts:160-165` — on an Origin mismatch it logs `logger.warn` and `return null`, and null means pass. Because the site configures `proxy: { origin }` (index.ts:201) the `expectedOriginConfigured` short-circuit at L133-147 is indeed not what fires, exactly as the finding states; execution reaches the mismatch branch. I confirmed a concrete cross-site attack shape: a page on evil.com auto-submitting `POST https://mochi.fast/demos/email/` (`preset=welcome`) or `/demos/queue/` is accepted and runs the action, where production mode returns 403. Note a corollary that supports the "unintended side effect" reading — `origin` is built from `MOCHI_DOMAIN`/`MOCHI_PORT`, neither set in the Dockerfile, so it resolves to `http://localhost:3333`, meaning the dev bypass is currently what keeps the site's own legitimate forms working at all. I downgrade HIGH→MEDIUM on blast radius, which I checked rather than assumed: `packages/demos` declares zero form actions and zero mutating POST routes (hn/todo/admin routes are all GET pages plus one read-only API), and on `packages/site` the only credential-bearing cookie is the login demo's, set with `sameSite: 'Lax'` (demos/login/routes.ts:28), which browsers do not send on a cross-site POST — so no privilege-bearing cross-site mutation is demonstrable today. The control being globally off on an internet-facing deployment is still real, and the Dockerfile is the reference pattern a framework user would copy.

Same root cause as F1 but a materially different exposure and a different fix, so I am not marking it duplicate. The stack-trace leak is real and trivially reachable: `errors.ts:93-96` attaches `thrown.stack` to the error page's props when `development`, and `templates/DefaultError.svelte` renders it verbatim in a `<pre>` under a "Stack trace" heading. The site sets no `errorPage`, so that default is in use, and `packages/site/src/demos/error/routes.ts` registers `/demos/error/500` on `Error500.svelte`, whose script is literally `throw new Error(...)` — so an anonymous `GET https://mochi.fast/demos/error/500/` renders a full stack trace with container-absolute paths. All three internal route families are confirmed live: `debugBarEnabled = development && (options.debugBar ?? true)` is true (site sets no `debugBar`), mounting `buildClientStatsRoutes` (`/_mochi/client/stats`, disclosing `getClientStats()` = every bundle output's input paths and sizes) and `buildPageCacheAdminRoutes` (`/__mochi/admin/page-cache` + `/stats` + `/entries`, with `purgeAll`/`purge` actions); `emailViewerEnabled = development && transport==='dev'` is true because `email/config.ts:12` defaults the transport to `dev` in development and the site passes no `email` option. Two corrections, neither of which changes the verdict. (1) The finding's mitigation "neither deployed site has any sendEmail caller" is wrong — it grepped the internal symbol; the public API is `Mochi.email()`, and `packages/site/src/demos/email/routes.ts` calls it from two form actions, so `/_mochi/email` on mochi.fast is populated. The disclosed content is harmless (fixed server-side presets to the hardcoded `ada@example.com`), but the viewer, its `clear` action and the attachment byte-stream are genuinely live, not inert. (2) `Mochi.ts:527-528` attaches `err.stack` to the `mochiEvents.emit('error')` payload — server-side observability, not an HTTP body — and `Mochi.ts:743` returns only `err.message`; the client-visible stack leak is errors.ts:93 and Mochi.ts:1639. I also found unmentioned corroboration: `Mochi.ts:1731-1765` mounts `/_mochi/image-cache` under the same `debugBarEnabled` gate as a raw Bun route (bypassing `buildRequestContext`, so no CSRF and no protection gate), where a bare POST calls `cache.clearAll()` — an unauthenticated purge that forces re-transcoding of every image. I confirmed the page-cache admin is hardcoded stubs with no-op purges, as the finding states. MEDIUM is right: the aggregate (anonymous stack traces, an unauthenticated image-cache purge, a standing `admin`-named surface) is real, while confidentiality impact is blunted because the repo and Dockerfile are public, so the disclosed layout is largely already known.

The code facts are all correct — L55 sets `HEAP_SNAPSHOTS_ENABLED=true`, `packages/site/src/routes.ts:90` reads exactly that, and L156-172 registers `/_heapsnapshot` as a bare `Mochi.api()` that returns `Bun.generateHeapSnapshot('v8')` with no credential check — but there is no reachable attack in the as-shipped, as-documented configuration, for four verified reasons. First, `EXPOSE` (L58) publishes nothing; it is image metadata, and the finding treats it as contributing to exposure, which is wrong. Second, both documented launch paths run with no `-p`: the header comment at L12, and `memtest/run.sh` L18, which defaults `PUBLISH` to empty and only adds `-p` when the operator sets it. The port therefore lives in the container's own netns, where the sole client is the driver the ENTRYPOINT starts. Third, this is not an accepted-risk-by-omission but an explicitly reasoned one: `memtest/run.sh` L14-17 and `memtest/README.md` both document the hazard by endpoint name — "publishing would expose /_heapsnapshot (a full heap dump) and /__mochi/health/memory to the network" — and offer `PUBLISH=127.0.0.1` for loopback-only access. That is the same category as this project's other documented deliberate trade-offs. Fourth, the impact claim collapses on inspection: `.dockerignore` excludes `.env*`, `run.sh` passes only `-e PORT` and `-e MEMTEST_GIT_SHA`, and `mochiConfig.ts:31-42` generates a random ephemeral key when `MOCHI_KEY` is unset — so this throwaway container holds no real MOCHI_KEY, no SMTP credentials, no ADMIN_PASSWORD and no database, and dumping its heap yields nothing that crosses a trust boundary. I also confirmed the image is never built or pushed by CI (build.yml's matrix is site/demos/support only; no workflow references Dockerfile.memtest), so it is local operator tooling, not a deployment. The framework-level question of whether an unauthenticated heap-dump route should exist behind only an env flag is a fair hardening discussion, but as a finding against this Dockerfile it is not exploitable.

Not a duplicate of F3: a different env var on a different line (53 vs 55), enabling a different endpoint in different code (framework `Mochi.ts` vs site `routes.ts`) with a different impact class (availability vs disclosure), so I give it its own verdict. The code is as described — `Mochi.ts:1816-1824` registers `/__mochi/health/memory` on `process.env.MOCHI_MEMORY_PROBE === '1'` as a raw Bun route with no auth, no rate limit and no `buildRequestContext`, and the handler calls the synchronous stop-the-world `Bun.gc(true)` on every request before returning `process.memoryUsage()`. But the DoS requires network reach to that port, and the reachability analysis is identical to F3 and fails the same way: `EXPOSE` publishes nothing, and neither documented invocation (`Dockerfile.memtest` L12, `memtest/run.sh` which leaves `PUBLISH` empty by default) maps it to a host address, so the only client is the driver running inside the same container. `memtest/run.sh` L14-17 names this exact endpoint as the reason the port stays unpublished. Beyond reachability, the impact premise does not survive contact with the image's purpose: this container exists to hammer the site with `CONCURRENCY=8` sitemap requests continuously for days on a dedicated box, the driver itself already calls the probe on a 5-minute cadence by design (`MEM_LOG_INTERVAL_MS`), and there is no service whose availability matters to deny. The memory figures it discloses are the harness's own telemetry about a throwaway process. Whether the framework should gate `MOCHI_MEMORY_PROBE` behind a secret is a reasonable defence-in-depth suggestion, but no concrete attack exists against this Dockerfile as written.

Verified exactly as described, and the in-repo evidence is actually stronger than the finding cites. Dockerfile.production L32-35 copies only package directories, L36 synthesizes a narrowed root manifest with `printf`, and L37 runs `bun install --production --omit=dev` — no `bun.lock` ever reaches `/temp/prod`, and the L28-29 comment confirms the regeneration is deliberate. With no lockfile present Bun re-resolves every direct and transitive dependency from the registry against the semver ranges at image-build time, with no integrity pins and no lockfile diff for a reviewer to see. The inconsistency the finding calls the tell is worse than two-of-three: the root `Dockerfile` (L29/31) and `Dockerfile.memtest` (L21/23) both do `COPY package.json bun.lock` + `--frozen-lockfile`, and `packages/demos/Dockerfile.production` (L9/17) does `COPY package.json bun.lock` + `bun install --frozen-lockfile --production --omit=dev` — so three of four get it right, and the exact clean pattern the recommendation asks for already exists in this repo. Only the one image carrying real secrets omits it: build.yml L67-74 makes `support` the sole leg on Dockerfile.production, and that app holds `ADMIN_PASSWORD`, `SMTP_*` and the subscriber database. Its tree is caret-ranged (`svelte: ^5.57.3`, `@nprapps/sidechain: ^1.1.5`, plus the whole `mochi-framework` tree), so the attack path is concrete and matches real 2025 npm incidents: one malicious in-range patch release lands in the image and runs in the process holding those credentials. One correction that trims the escalation without touching the verdict — Bun does not execute arbitrary lifecycle scripts by default (only for its default-trusted list or declared `trustedDependencies`), so the "postinstall executes inside CI" step is weaker than stated; the durable exposure is the unreviewed runtime code and the loss of a reproducible build for forensics. The base-image digest suggestion is fair hardening but not a finding on its own, since `BUN_IMAGE` is already version-pinned. MEDIUM is appropriate given the secrets involved and the trivial fix.
